hints: Focus on what is actually in the beaker after the carbonates dissolve in nitric acid, both metals will now be present as soluble nitrates.
Recall your solubility rules for chlorides and sulfates, especially how barium and magnesium behave differently with sulfate ions.
Look for the reagent that makes one metal form an insoluble solid while the other stays dissolved, so filtration can separate them.
walkthrough:
**Identify what is in solution**

Great start, let's see what dissolving does. Both carbonates react with nitric acid to give soluble nitrates, water and carbon dioxide.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{MgCO}_3 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Mg(NO}_3)_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{BaCO}_3 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Think about how separation works**

To get a separate magnesium compound and barium compound, you need selective precipitation. One ion must form an insoluble solid, while the other stays in solution so you can filter them apart.

**Apply solubility rules**

Remember, all nitrates are soluble and almost all chlorides are soluble, including $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{BaCl}_2$. For sulfates, most are soluble but barium sulfate is a famous exception.

Key rule:
$$\text{BaSO}_4 \text{ is insoluble (white precipitate), } \text{MgSO}_4 \text{ is soluble}$$

**Choose the correct reagent**

Adding dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$ precipitates barium as solid $\text{BaSO}_4$, which can be filtered off. Magnesium stays in the filtrate as soluble $\text{MgSO}_4$, giving you two separate compounds.

options.A: Incorrect. Both $\text{BaCl}_2$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$ are soluble in water, so adding $\text{HCl}(aq)$ gives no precipitate to filter off. This traps students who assume barium chloride is insoluble like silver chloride.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{MgCl}_2$ is very soluble, so no solid magnesium chloride will form. Adding $\text{HCl}(aq)$ leaves both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in solution with no separation.
options.C: Correct. Adding $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$ gives $\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$, an insoluble white precipitate that can be filtered off. $\text{MgSO}_4$ remains soluble in the filtrate, so you have cleanly separated the barium compound from the magnesium compound.
options.D: Incorrect. It correctly identifies $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$ as the reagent, but gets the solubility the wrong way round. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble and stays in solution, it is $\text{BaSO}_4$ that is the filterable solid.
